content: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with hydroxychloroquine. Exercise caution when administering hydroxychloroquine to nursing women. Published lactation data indicate that hydroxychloroquine is present in human milk at low levels. No adverse reactions have been reported in breastfed infants, and no retinal toxicity, ototoxicity, cardiotoxicity, or growth and developmental abnormalities have been observed in children exposed to hydroxychloroquine through breast milk. There is no information available regarding the effect of hydroxychloroquine on milk production. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. When administered to nursing women, hydroxychloroquine is excreted in human milk, and it is known that infants are highly sensitive to the toxic effects of 4-aminoquinolines. Hydroxychloroquine is generally considered acceptable for use during pregnancy. Controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. The drug has a half-life of 40–50 days and is metabolized into desethylhydroxychloroquine and desethylchloroquine. When taking hydroxychloroquine, it should be consumed with a meal or a glass of milk. Tablets should not be crushed or split. The medication should be dispensed in a tight, light-resistant container and kept out of the reach of children. It should be stored at room temperature (20–25°C [68–77°F]), with allowable excursions between 15–30°C (59–86°F). The information provided is for general informational and educational purposes only.
